KEY MESSAGE 1...Frost concerns for portions of the area early 
this morning.

High pressure extending from Maine down to Virginia. The
combination of clear skies and light winds allowed temperatures
to drop into the 30s. However, the pressure gradient will begin
to tighten between that high and low pressure off the Mid-
Atlantic coast lifting to the north. North to northeast winds
will increase to around 10 mph by daybreak, limiting
temperatures from falling much farther. As a result, really not
looking for a hard freeze to develop, but frost is likely,
especially north and west of the I-95 corridor. Frost Advisories
remain in effect through 9 am.

After a cold start to the day, high temperatures rebound into
the low to mid 60s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A nor'easter developing off the coast of the 
southern Mid-Atlantic is expected to bring coastal impacts and 
create hazardous marine conditions through at least the middle 
of this week.

As an upper-trough continues to shift eastward away from the 
Eastern Seaboard, a portion of it has become cutoff from the 
parent trough and is in the process of becoming a closed low at 
this time. Strong and expansive high pressure is building over 
the Ohio Valley and into portions of the Northeast. Latest 
surface analysis indicates that an area of surface low pressure 
has formed off the coast of the Carolinas, and it will track 
generally northeastward over the next several days off the 
coast. 

Overall, confidence has increased that through at least 
Wednesday, the nor'easter will remain close enough to bring 
multiple impacts to our coastal areas. Persistently strong 
northeast winds will push water towards the coast. Multiple 
rounds of coastal flooding are likely (see key message 3 below).
Increasing seas may result in beach erosion in some areas as 
well. For areas along the immediate coast, gusty winds up to 
around 30-35 mph are possible. Inland, impacts are expected to 
be quite limited with how far offshore the storm is likely to 
be. In fact, outside of a few showers at the coast, little to no
precipitation is likely at all over land areas.

For Thursday and beyond, there appears to be a growing 
consensus in model guidance that the storm will begin to shift 
farther east out to sea, lessening marine and coastal impacts. 
Both the ECENS and GEFS suites feature the low making its 
closest approach by Thursday morning and then moving away, 
though there are still a few members of each that indicate it 
could remain around for longer. These appear to be becoming 
outliers however.


KEY MESSAGE 3...A prolonged period of onshore flow will lead to 
multiple elevated high tide cycles this week resulting in rounds of 
coastal flooding.

As the nor'easter develops and meanders offshore through at
least the middle of the week, there will be a persistent and 
strong northeast wind in place. This will lead to a prolonged 
period of onshore flow resulting in multiple elevated high tide 
cycles. The first high tide cycle of concern is currently 
expected to be Tuesday evening as spotty minor to minor tidal 
flooding is forecast. A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect
for the Tuesday evening high tide cycle for Ocean, southeastern
Burlington, Atlantic, Cape May, Kent, and Sussex County 
Delaware. This Advisory goes from 3 PM to 9 PM Tuesday and is 
for widespread minor coastal flooding. 

The high tide cycle late Tuesday night into early Wednesday 
morning, looks to bring another round of spotty minor to 
widespread minor tidal flooding. An additional Coastal Flood 
Advisory will likely be needed for Ocean, southeastern 
Burlington, Atlantic, Cape May, Kent, and Sussex County 
Delaware.

Additional coastal flood hazards will likely be needed for high
tide cycles Wednesday, and potentially Thursday, as the high 
tide cycles remain elevated. From the current forecast, 
Wednesday evening's high tide cycle looks to be the one of most 
concern with widespread minor to low-end moderate coastal 
flooding. Beyond Wednesday evening, another round of coastal 
flooding is possible but uncertainty remains in the exact extent
as it will be dependent on the location of the nor'easter.
